lead: A fiber does not decide on its own whether it is single-mode. The wavelength does. Compare the core size with the wavelength through one dimensionless number, V, and the fiber is single-mode only while V stays below 2.405. Push the wavelength shorter and V rises, more field patterns appear, and they interfere. This one inequality sets the cutoff wavelength of every step-index fiber, and it decides whether a link uses a cheap LED over 300 m or a laser over 80 km.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for what a mode is, and Chapter 1.5 for the core radius and index step.

sections.h3: The V number and the single-mode condition

blocks.text: A step-index fiber has a core of radius a and index n1, inside a cladding of index n2. The numerical aperture NA measures how strongly the guide pulls light in (Chapter 1.3). One dimensionless number collects the geometry and the wavelength:

blocks.where: V is the normalized frequency (dimensionless); a is the core radius in µm; λ is the free-space wavelength in µm; NA is the numerical aperture, dimensionless.

blocks.text: V compares the core circumference 2πa with the wavelength, weighted by NA. A large V means the core is many wavelengths wide, so many modes fit. A small V means the field barely fits, so only one mode survives.
For a step-index fiber at large V, the number of guided modes is about M ≈ V²/2. Each mode is a distinct field pattern from Chapter 1.4. The exact condition for single-mode operation is:

blocks.where: 2.405 is the first zero of the Bessel function J₀. It is the V value at which the second mode, LP<sub>11</sub>, reaches cutoff.

blocks.text: Below V = 2.405 only the fundamental mode LP<sub>01</sub> travels. Single-mode does not mean one ray: many rays still bounce inside the core, but they all add up to the same field pattern.
The cutoff wavelength is the λ at which V equals 2.405. Put V = 2.405 and solve for λ:

blocks.where: λ<sub>c</sub> is the cutoff wavelength in µm; a is the core radius in µm; NA is the numerical aperture.

blocks.text: Above cutoff, λ > λc, V falls below 2.405 and the fiber is single-mode. Below cutoff, λ < λc, V is larger, several modes travel, and they interfere at the receiver as modal noise (Chapter 1.5).
So a fiber is not single-mode by itself. It is single-mode at wavelengths longer than its own cutoff, and the same fiber used at a shorter wavelength becomes multimode.

Take a = 4 µm and NA = 0.11. Then 2πa·NA = 2.7646 µm and λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.15 µm. At 1.31 µm, V = 2.11, so the fiber is single-mode. At 0.85 µm, V = 3.25, so it is multimode. Single-mode fiber is designed with λ<sub>c</sub> near 1.1–1.3 µm so that both the 1.31 µm and the 1.55 µm windows stay single-mode.

sections.h3: Mode field diameter and the multimode family

blocks.text: In a single-mode fiber the field is not strictly inside the core. The mode field diameter (MFD) is the diameter at which the intensity falls to 1/e² of its peak on axis. It is typically 9–10 µm at 1.55 µm, slightly larger than the core. MFD, not core diameter, sets splice loss and bending loss (Unit 5, Link Design and Fiber Measurements). With one mode there is no intermodal dispersion, so single-mode fiber carries the highest bit rates over long distances. It needs a laser and tight connector tolerances.
Multimode fiber has V well above 2.405, so hundreds or thousands of modes travel.

blocks.text: In graded-index fiber the index falls smoothly from centre to cladding. A ray that swings far from the axis spends its time in lower-index glass, where light travels faster, so it catches up with the axial ray. Intermodal dispersion shrinks, and a few hundred metres at multi-Gb/s becomes possible with a cheap source.

examples.question: A step-index fiber has core radius a = 4.0 µm and numerical aperture NA = 0.11. (a) Find its cutoff wavelength. (b) At an operating wavelength of 1.31 µm, is the fiber single-mode? Support your answer with V.
steps: Write the normalized frequency: V = 2πa·NA / λ.
Compute the constant numerator: 2π × 4.0 µm × 0.11 = 2.7646 µm. NA is dimensionless, so the unit stays µm.
At λ = 1.31 µm: V = 2.7646 µm / 1.31 µm = 2.110, dimensionless.
Compare: 2.11 < 2.405, so only the fundamental mode travels. The fiber is single-mode at 1.31 µm.
examples.answer: The cutoff wavelength is 1.15 µm, and at 1.31 µm the fiber has V = 2.11 < 2.405, so it is single-mode.
examples.check:
import math
a = 4.0
NA = 0.11
k = 2 * math.pi * a * NA
lc = k / 2.405
V = k / 1.31
print(round(lc, 2))
print(round(V, 2))

code.code:
import math

a = 4.0        # core radius, micrometres
NA = 0.11      # numerical aperture, dimensionless

k = 2 * math.pi * a * NA
lc = k / 2.405
V_131 = k / 1.31

print("2*pi*a*NA =", round(k, 4), "micrometres")
print("cutoff wavelength =", round(lc, 2), "micrometres")
print("V at 1.31 micrometres =", round(V_131, 2))
print("single-mode?", V_131 < 2.405)

traps: Single-mode means λ is longer than λ<sub>c</sub>, so V is smaller than 2.405. A wavelength shorter than cutoff gives multimode operation, not single-mode.
V is dimensionless. Do not write V in µm or nm; only a and λ carry length units, and they must be in the same unit.
Cutoff wavelength depends on a and NA only. It does not change with source power, fiber length, or the number of connectors.
Do not confuse cutoff wavelength with the operating wavelength. A fiber sold as single-mode at 1.31 µm has its λ<sub>c</sub> below 1.31 µm, not equal to it.
2.405 is the LP<sub>11</sub> cutoff, not an arbitrary constant. The fundamental LP<sub>01</sub> mode has no cutoff in a step-index fiber.

quiz.q: Define the normalized frequency V for a step-index fiber and state the single-mode condition.
quiz.a: V = (2πa/λ)·NA, where a is the core radius, λ the free-space wavelength and NA the numerical aperture. Single-mode when V < 2.405.

quiz.q: Why does V decrease when the wavelength is increased, and what does that do to the number of guided modes?
quiz.a: V is proportional to a/λ, so a longer wavelength makes the core look electrically smaller and V falls. The mode count M ≈ V²/2 falls with it, until below 2.405 only LP<sub>01</sub> is guided.

quiz.q: A step-index fiber has a = 5.0 µm and NA = 0.20. Find λ<sub>c</sub>. At λ = 1.55 µm, is it single-mode?
quiz.a: 2πa·NA = 2π × 5.0 × 0.20 = 6.2832 µm. λ<sub>c</sub> = 6.2832/2.405 = 2.61 µm. At 1.55 µm, V = 6.2832/1.55 = 4.05, which is greater than 2.405, so the fiber is multimode.

quiz.q: Two fibers have the same NA = 0.11 but core radii 4 µm and 8 µm. Compare their behaviour at 1.31 µm.
quiz.a: λ<sub>c</sub> scales with a, so the 8 µm fiber has λ<sub>c</sub> ≈ 2.30 µm and V = 2 × 2.7646/1.31 = 4.22 at 1.31 µm, above 2.405: multimode. The 4 µm fiber has V = 2.11 and is single-mode. Larger core means more modes at the same wavelength.
The diameter at which the intensity of the fundamental mode falls to 1/e² of its peak value. It is slightly larger than the core diameter and sets splice and bending loss.

quiz.q: Why does graded-index multimode fiber have less intermodal dispersion than step-index multimode fiber?
quiz.a: The index falls smoothly from the axis, so rays travelling away from the axis spend time in lower-index glass where light moves faster. Their longer path is partly compensated, and the arrival times of different modes come closer together.

quiz.q: Why is single-mode fiber preferred for long-haul links even though its core is harder to handle?
quiz.a: Only one mode travels, so there is no intermodal dispersion and pulses stay sharp over tens of kilometres. That allows high bit rates, and the low-loss 1.55 µm window can be used. The cost is a small core and MFD, which demand lasers and precise splicing, but for long spans that cost is worth it.

quiz.q: A fiber is specified as single-mode at 1.31 µm. What can you say about its cutoff wavelength?
quiz.a: Its cutoff wavelength is below 1.31 µm, so that 1.31 µm lies in the single-mode region where V < 2.405.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real single-mode fibers follow standard designs such as ITU-T G.652 for ordinary long haul and G.657 for bend-insensitive indoor cable, where the MFD and cutoff are tightly specified. When a link must carry several independent modes on purpose, few-mode fiber is used with multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) digital signal processing, a research route to higher capacity. Hollow-core fibers, which guide light mostly in air, are another active area because they promise lower latency and lower loss. Search next for mode field diameter measurement, bend-insensitive fiber, and few-mode fiber MIMO.
